steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper studying how the complexity of instruction-tuning data relates to LLM alignment. It should motivate the open questions about complexity, introduce our Tree-Instruct method for controlled complexity increases, and summarize our preliminary findings.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- LLMs and instruction tuning
- Instruction data quality; complexity as an under-explored factor; three open questions
- Hurdle: increasing complexity without adding diversity (WizardLM's in-depth evolving)
- Tree-Instruct: adding nodes to the semantic tree
- Preliminary conclusions (1)-(3)

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- LLMs and instruction tuning
  - new LLMs get attention for potential in language technologies
  - instruction-tuning on supervised input-output pairs for chat/user requests
  - teaches style and format, shows knowledge/capabilities from pre-training
- Instruction data and complexity
  - instruction data quality shapes LLM abilities and user perception
  - LIMA: 1000 curated prompts/responses -> strong performance
  - => scaling not only quantity; diversity and quality matter
  - complexity less explored; three questions:
    - (1) scaling law of instruction complexity: complex data may elicit more capability; WizardLM in-depth/in-breadth evolving, 12.4% win rate increase, same data amount; complexity vs diversity unclear; further complexity increases unexplored
    - (2) complexity vs token quantity: more complexity -> more tokens per instance; WizardLM same instance count but more tokens; more pretraining tokens -> better performance
    - (3) complexity-based curriculum: easy -> hard; works in machine translation, dialogue, QA; untested for instruction tuning
- Hurdle
  - need controlled complexity increase without diversity
  - WizardLM in-depth evolving prompt [quote: WizardLM's in-depth evolving prompt]
  - may drift from original objective -> diversity; worse when repeated
  - analysis in Sec. 4.1; Fig. 2: evolved instructions append extra objectives
- Tree-Instruct
  - LLM adds a specific number of new nodes to instruction's semantic tree, not text sequence (unlike Self-Instruct, WizardLM)
  - number of added nodes = complexity level
  - tree nodes have no sequential order -> like inserting words in the middle
  - keeps structure of original instruction, less straying from theme
  - GPT-4 consistency check: WizardLM 0.56 -> 0.69
  - Fig. 1: added nodes raise complexity
- Conclusions
  - (1) benefits grow with complexity: following LIMA, 1,000 Alpaca-GPT-4 samples; add 3, 6, 10 nodes -> 13%, 20%, 26% gains over eight sub-skills (commonsense, writing, coding); extends to ~6,000 ShareGPT conversations via OpenChat; ~1,100 instructions complicated; AlpacaEval win rate 84.56% -> 86.19%
  - (2) partly from tokens, but few complex beat many simple at same token budget: ten nodes -> avg tokens 186 -> 607; originals 1,000 -> 4,000 to match tokens; still >15% gain; complexity equivalent to diversity of four times token count; same tokens: 2% higher win rate than three iterations of WizardLM in-depth evolution
  - (3) curriculum may not help: easy (three nodes) -> medium (six) -> hard (ten); beats mixed difficulty with same steps but loses to ten-node only; simple samples matter less

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
The newest large language models (LLMs) have got a lot of attention because of their huge potential in language technologies. To make them better at interactive user requests and chat interfaces, these models are instruction-tuned on supervised input-output pairs. This lets the model understand which style and format it needs for interacting with users well, and it shows the knowledge and capabilities that the model got during pre-training.

So the quality of the instruction data has a big influence on what LLMs can do, and it shapes how users see their capabilities. Recently LIMA showed that an LLM can get remarkably strong performance with only 1000 carefully curated prompts and responses. This suggests that the scaling laws of instruction tuning do not only depend on how much data there is, but are also influenced by how diverse and good the prompts are. However, one important aspect of evaluating instruction data that is less explored is complexity. There are at least three open questions about complexity. (1) The scaling law of instruction complexity. Intuitively, more complex instruction data might bring out more of the potential capabilities of LLMs to solve intricate problems. WizardLM introduces in-depth and in-breadth evolving methods that rewrite prompts into more complex and diverse versions, and this gives a 12.4% increase in the win rate of LLMs with the same amount of data. But it is still uncertain whether WizardLM's improvement comes from complexity or just from diversity. Also, continuing to increase the complexity has not been explored yet. (2) The relationship between the performance improvement from complexity and the number of tokens. Making an instance more complex inevitably increases how many tokens it has. WizardLM improves performance with the same number of instances, but it increases the number of tokens per instance. So the question is whether the improvement from complexity is actually because of more training tokens. It is known that more pretraining tokens can make LLMs perform better. (3) Whether curriculum instruction learning based on complexity is effective. Curriculum learning is a machine learning strategy that starts with easy instances and slowly introduces harder ones. It has been shown to work in different NLP tasks such as machine translation, dialogue systems, and question answering. But whether it can work for instruction tuning is still under-explored.

But to answer these questions, the main hurdle is to find a controlled way of increasing the complexity of instruction data that does not bring in unwanted factors like diversity. WizardLM uses an in-depth evolving prompt like “ Your objective is to rewrite a given prompt into a more complex version to make ChatGPT and GPT4 a bit harder to handle. ” to make existing instructions more complicated. Unfortunately, even though this approach is meant to increase complexity, it might also bring in diversity by accident, because it can move away from what the original instruction was trying to do. This problem gets especially bad when in-depth evolving is used again and again to reach different levels of complexity. We study the instructions before and after in-depth evolving in Sec. 4.1. As Fig. 2 shows, the instructions evolved over several iterations add extra objectives that go away from the original instructions, which shows more diversity.

- Tree-Instruct
  - LLM adds a specific number of new nodes to the instruction's semantic tree, not the text sequence (unlike Self-Instruct, WizardLM)
  - number of added nodes = level of complexity
  - tree nodes have no sequential order -> like inserting words into the middle
  - keeps structural constraints of original, less drift from main theme
  - GPT-4 consistency score: WizardLM 0.56 -> 0.69; Fig. 1
- Preliminary conclusions
  - (1) benefits keep growing with complexity: following LIMA, 1,000 Alpaca-GPT-4 samples; 3, 6, 10 nodes -> 13%, 20%, 26% over eight sub-skills (commonsense, writing, coding); ~6,000 ShareGPT conversations via OpenChat, ~1,100 instructions complicated; AlpacaEval 84.56% -> 86.19%
  - (2) partly tokens, but few complex beat diverse simple at same token budget: avg tokens 186 -> 607 with ten nodes; originals 1,000 -> 4,000; still >15% gain; equals diversity of four times token count; 2% higher win rate than three WizardLM in-depth iterations
  - (3) curriculum may not be effective: three -> six -> ten nodes; beats mixed difficulty, loses to ten-node only; simple samples matter less

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
The newest large language models (LLMs) have got a lot of attention because of their huge potential in language technologies. To make them better at interactive user requests and chat interfaces, these models are instruction-tuned on supervised input-output pairs. This lets the model understand which style and format it needs for interacting with users well, and it shows the knowledge and capabilities that the model got during pre-training.

So the quality of the instruction data has a big influence on what LLMs can do, and it shapes how users see their capabilities. Recently LIMA showed that an LLM can get remarkably strong performance with only 1000 carefully curated prompts and responses. This suggests that the scaling laws of instruction tuning do not only depend on how much data there is, but are also influenced by how diverse and good the prompts are. However, one important aspect of evaluating instruction data that is less explored is complexity. There are at least three open questions about complexity. (1) The scaling law of instruction complexity. Intuitively, more complex instruction data might bring out more of the potential capabilities of LLMs to solve intricate problems. WizardLM introduces in-depth and in-breadth evolving methods that rewrite prompts into more complex and diverse versions, and this gives a 12.4% increase in the win rate of LLMs with the same amount of data. But it is still uncertain whether WizardLM's improvement comes from complexity or just from diversity. Also, continuing to increase the complexity has not been explored yet. (2) The relationship between the performance improvement from complexity and the number of tokens. Making an instance more complex inevitably increases how many tokens it has. WizardLM improves performance with the same number of instances, but it increases the number of tokens per instance. So the question is whether the improvement from complexity is actually because of more training tokens. It is known that more pretraining tokens can make LLMs perform better. (3) Whether curriculum instruction learning based on complexity is effective. Curriculum learning is a machine learning strategy that starts with easy instances and slowly introduces harder ones. It has been shown to work in different NLP tasks such as machine translation, dialogue systems, and question answering. But whether it can work for instruction tuning is still under-explored.

But to answer these questions, the main hurdle is to find a controlled way of increasing the complexity of instruction data that does not bring in unwanted factors like diversity. WizardLM uses an in-depth evolving prompt like “ Your objective is to rewrite a given prompt into a more complex version to make ChatGPT and GPT4 a bit harder to handle. ” to make existing instructions more complicated. Unfortunately, even though this approach is meant to increase complexity, it might also bring in diversity by accident, because it can move away from what the original instruction was trying to do. This problem gets especially bad when in-depth evolving is used again and again to reach different levels of complexity. We study the instructions before and after in-depth evolving in Sec. 4.1. As Fig. 2 shows, the instructions evolved over several iterations add extra objectives that go away from the original instructions, which shows more diversity.

To deal with this, we propose Tree-Instruct. It prompts LLMs to add a specific number of new nodes to the semantic tree of an existing instruction, instead of changing the text sequence directly like Self-Instruct or WizardLM do. The number of added nodes is used to represent how much complexity is introduced. The advantage of this is that the nodes of a semantic tree do not have any sequential order. When the LLM is forced to work on the semantic tree, the process becomes like inserting new words in the middle of the original instruction. This makes the model add complexity while keeping to the structural constraints of the original instruction, instead of just appending new instructions at the end. This can strongly reduce the problem of moving away from the main theme of the original instruction. We use GPT-4 to judge how consistent the evolved instructions are with the original ones, and the results confirm that Tree-Instruct raises the consistency score of WizardLM from 0.56 to 0.69. Fig. 1 shows how the number of added nodes increases the complexity level of the samples.

Using Tree-Instruct, we got the following preliminary conclusions from experiments:

(1) When the complexity of the instruction data goes up, the benefits of instruction tuning keep growing. Following LIMA, we try instruction tuning with 1,000 samples from Alpaca-GPT-4 as a base. We add 3, 6, and 10 nodes to the semantic tree of each sample, and this gives performance gains of 13%, 20%, and 26%, across eight sub-skills like commonsense, writing, and coding, so the improvements are consistent. This scaling law also extends to more complex instruction data. For example, when we fine-tune on around 6,000 conversations filtered from ShareGPT via OpenChat (which performs very well among open-source LLMs), we see that if we increase the complexity of around 1,100 users' instructions with Tree-Instruct, the win rate on the AlpacaEval benchmark goes up from 84.56% to 86.19%.

(2) Part of the increase from complexity comes from extra tokens, but a few complex instructions do better than diverse but simple instructions under the same token budget. We see that as complexity increases, the number of tokens increases too. Adding ten nodes to the semantic tree increases the average token length of instructions from 186 to 607. So, to make the comparison fair, we increase the number of original instructions from 1,000 to 4,000 so that the total number of tokens matches our tree-instructed samples. In this setting, adding ten nodes still gives more than 15% performance gain. This shows that the improvement from complexity is partly because of more tokens, but making samples more complex is equivalent to the diversity you get from four times the token count of simple samples. Also, with the same number of instruction tokens, Tree-Instruct evolution gets a 2% higher win rate than three iterations of WizardLM's in-depth evolution, which shows Tree-Instruct is better at increasing complexity.

(3) Curriculum instruction tuning may not be effective, and increasing complexity is all you need. We do curriculum learning by training the LLM on increasing levels of difficulty step by step. First we train on easy-level data with three nodes added, then on medium-level data with six nodes, and at the end on hard data with ten nodes added. We see that with the same number of training steps, curriculum learning does do better than training on samples with mixed difficulty, but it is still worse than training only on the instruction data with ten added nodes. This shows that as the complexity of samples increases, the simpler samples become much less important, and it suggests that repeating the training with complex samples may be enough.

steps.text:
The latest generation of large language models (LLMs) has attracted significant attention due to their great potential in language technologies [1,2,3,4]. To better handle interactive user requests and chat interfaces, these models undergo instruction-tuning on supervised input-output pairs [5,6,7]. This process lets the model learn the style and format required for effective user interaction, showcasing the knowledge and capabilities gained during pre-training [8].

Consequently, the efficacy of instruction data strongly influences LLMs' abilities and shapes users' perceptions of their capabilities [9,10,11]. Recently, LIMA has shown that with just 1000 carefully curated prompts and responses, an LLM can achieve remarkably strong performance [12]. This suggests that the scaling laws of instruction tuning do not depend solely on data quantity but are also influenced by prompt diversity and quality. However, one critical and less-explored aspect of evaluating instruction data is complexity. There are at least three unanswered questions related to complexity: (1) The scaling law of instruction complexity: Intuitively, more complex instruction data might elicit more potential capabilities in LLMs to address intricate problems [13,14]. WizardLM [15] introduces in-depth and in-breadth evolving methods to rewrite prompts into more complex and diverse versions, resulting in a 12.4% increase in LLMs' win rate with the same amount of data. Yet it remains uncertain whether WizardLM's performance improvement is due to complexity or merely to diversity. Moreover, continued increases in complexity are yet to be explored. (2) The relationship between complexity-induced performance improvement and token quantity: Increasing instance complexity inevitably increases the number of tokens per instance [16]. While WizardLM improves performance with the same number of instances, it increases the number of tokens per instance. This raises the question of whether complexity-induced improvement in LLMs simply results from more training tokens, since enlarging LLMs' pretraining token counts is known to lead to better performance [17,18]. (3) The effectiveness of complexity-based curriculum instruction learning: Curriculum learning is a machine learning strategy that starts with easy instances and gradually introduces harder ones [19]. Its effectiveness has been demonstrated in various NLP tasks such as machine translation [20], dialogue systems [21], and question answering [22]. However, its potential in instruction tuning is still under-explored.

To answer these questions, however, the key hurdle is finding a controlled way to increase the complexity of instruction data without introducing unwanted factors such as diversity. WizardLM [15] uses an in-depth evolving prompt like “ Your objective is to rewrite a given prompt into a more complex version to make ChatGPT and GPT4 a bit harder to handle. ” to complicate existing instructions. Unfortunately, although it is intended to enhance complexity, this approach might inadvertently introduce diversity by diverting from the initial instruction objectives. The issue becomes particularly severe when in-depth evolving is applied repeatedly to reach varying levels of complexity. We study and analyze the instructions before and after in-depth evolving in Sec. 4.1. As illustrated in Fig. 2, the iteratively evolved instructions append additional objectives that deviate from the original instructions, showing greater diversity.

To address this concern, we propose Tree-Instruct, which prompts LLMs to add a specific number of new nodes to the semantic tree of an existing instruction, rather than manipulating the text sequence directly as Self-Instruct [23] or WizardLM [15] do. The number of added nodes represents the introduced level of complexity. The advantage of this approach is that semantic tree nodes lack any sequential order [24]. By forcing LLMs to operate on the semantic tree, the process becomes analogous to inserting new words into the middle of the original instruction. This compels the models to add complexity while adhering to the structural constraints of the initial instruction, rather than merely appending new instructions, and it can significantly mitigate the issue of straying from the primary theme of the initial instruction. We use GPT-4 to assess the consistency of evolved instructions with the original ones, and the results verify that Tree-Instruct improves WizardLM's consistency score from 0.56 to 0.69. Fig. 1 highlights how the number of added nodes raises the complexity level of the samples.

With the help of Tree-Instruct, we have obtained the following preliminary experimental conclusions:

(1) As the complexity of instruction data increases, the benefits of instruction tuning continue to grow: Following LIMA [12], we perform instruction tuning using 1,000 samples from Alpaca-GPT-4 as a base. We add 3, 6, and 10 nodes to the semantic tree of each sample, resulting in performance gains of 13%, 20%, and 26%, respectively, across eight sub-skills such as commonsense, writing, and coding, which shows consistent improvements. This scaling law also extends to more complex instruction data. For instance, when fine-tuning on around 6,000 conversations filtered from ShareGPT via OpenChat [25] (which performs excellently among open-source LLMs), we observe that increasing the complexity of around 1,100 users' instructions through Tree-Instruct raises the win rate on the AlpacaEval benchmark from 84.56% to 86.19%.

(2) The increase in complexity partly comes from additional tokens, but a few complex instructions outperform diverse yet simple instructions under the same token budget: We find that the number of tokens grows as the complexity increases. Adding ten nodes to the semantic tree increases the average token length of instructions from 186 to 607. Hence, for a fair comparison, we increase the number of original instructions from 1,000 to 4,000 to match the total token quantity of our tree-instructed samples. Under this setting, the performance gain from adding ten nodes is still more than 15%. This indicates that the improvement due to complexity is partly attributable to the increased tokens, but increasing sample complexity is equivalent to the diversity achieved by four times the token count of simple samples. Moreover, with an equal number of instruction tokens, Tree-Instruct evolution yields a 2% higher win rate than three iterations of WizardLM's in-depth evolution, demonstrating the superior efficacy of Tree-Instruct in enhancing complexity.

(3) Curriculum instruction tuning may not be effective; increasing complexity is all you need: We implement curriculum learning by training the LLM progressively on increasing levels of difficulty. We first train it on easy-level data with three added nodes, then on medium-level data with six nodes, and finally on hard data with ten added nodes. We observe that, given the same number of training steps, curriculum learning does outperform training on samples of mixed difficulty, but it still falls short of training solely on the ten-node instruction data. This indicates that the significance of simpler samples diminishes considerably as sample complexity increases, suggesting that repeated training on complex samples may be sufficient.
